Query: You are writing a feature essay for a publication on gaming history and culture. Your task is to analyze the key factors behind the long-term success of Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO).
Passage: Esports Essentials: The Impact of the Counter-Strike Majors

Esports Essentials is a series intended as an introduction to esports for anyone looking to understand the industry.

Counter-Strike has seen almost two decades of competitive play across multiple games. That competition has been headlined by events called Majors—high profile tournaments hosting the world's top teams. These Majors are also a core element to the game's long lifespan, as each year has seen over six figures in prizes across the various Majors.

So, how did Majors come to define top-level Counter-Strike competitions? Here's what you need to know.

What is the History Behind Majors?

There are essentially two eras when it comes to Counter-Strike. The first—better known as the time before the release of the franchise's most recent entry, Global Offensive (CS:GO)—lasted from 2001-2012.

The early years of esports were very different from today; most fans of pro-level play could only hang out in Internet Relay Chat (IRC) channels awaiting results and match replays. Before the rise of livestreaming, watching games live was only really possible in person. Despite all this, the very first Major—the 2001 Cyberathlete Professional League (CPL) Winter Championship—offered $150K in prize money.

CPL established itself with its Winter and Summer Majors, and was soon joined by Korea's World Cyber Games in 2002 and France's Electronic Sports World Cup in 2003. These four tournaments defined Counter-Strike esports through 2007, and contained some of the biggest rivalries between the game's top teams. When CPL folded in 2008, ESL stepped up and added Counter-Strike to its multi-game Intel Extreme Masters (IEM) series. These tournaments continued like clockwork for another four years.

What Changed in 2012?

For one, Global Offensive (CS:GO) was released. This new iteration was finally a strong enough replacement to get players to put down the original version of Counter-Strike, a feat neither of the franchise's previous entries (Condition Zero and Source) could match.

Gaming culture also dramatically shifted in 2012. While streaming gameplay had been possible for a few years (primarily on platforms like Ustream and Justin.tv), the launch of Twitch in 2011 meant big things for gaming. Just three years after it opened its digital doors, Twitch would be in the middle of a bidding war between Amazon and Google, finally selling to the former for $970 million.

"A portion of all sales from the eSports Weapon Case will be redirected to fund prize purses at upcoming CS:GO eSport events worldwide."

The final big change was that Counter-Strike developer Valve got involved in game's esports community. Previously, the game's esports scene was a minor interest to the game's developer—Valve was presumably preoccupied with its other franchises and building out the massive Steam marketplace. But while CS:GO signaled a massive change for the game's player base, it also embodied a massive shift in how the game's developer supported the esports scene.

This shift is seen clearly in the game's 2013 "Arms Deal" update, which added the extremely significant weapon skin system and marketplace. Part of this update, the eSports Weapon Case, hinted at big plans for the game's competitive future:

"A portion of all sales from the eSports Weapon Case will be redirected to fund prize purses at upcoming CS:GO eSport events worldwide."

Several weeks later, the shoe finally dropped. DreamHack announced CS:GO's first Major, a $250K tournament funded in part by those microtransactions. ESL soon rejoined the mix, adding its ESL One Katowice and Cologne stops as Majors as well.

Hours watched for the ELEAGUE Major 2018.

After two successful years, Valve started tapping other organizers to host Majors, starting with Major League Gaming (MLG) in 2016. This change also saw a raise in the prize pool offering to $1 million. Since then, ELEAGUE (2017, 2018), PGL (2017), and FACEIT (2018) have also been asked to host Majors. And, next year, Intel Extreme Masters will host another Major after a seven year break.

It's worth noting that the third-party hosts of Majors shifts every year, based on Valve's discretion. Every year, tournament organizers pitch the developer on who will be hosting one of the two available Majors.

What is the Current Format for a Major?

The most recent format implemented by Valve debuted at ELEAGUE's Boston 2018 Major, and takes part in three stages.

The New Challengers Stage features 16 teams, comprised of the bottom eight teams from the previous Major's New Legends Stage and eight teams from regional qualifiers (known as Minors). Eight teams advance from this stage into the New Legends Stage.

The New Legends Stage features 16 teams, comprised of the top eight teams from the New Challengers Stage and the "Current Legends"—the top eight teams from the previous Major's New Legends Stage. The top eight teams advance once more to the New Champions Stage.

The New Champions Stage features the top eight teams from the New Legends Stage, and is played out in a best-of-three single elimination bracket.

Notable throughout all of these formats is that Valve considers a team to be defined by the majority of its players, not the organization that has salaried or contracted them. Using a real world example: Team EnVyUs won ninth place at ELEAGUE's 2017 Major, but when three of EnVyUs' players transferred to G2 Esports later that year, G2 was given EnVyUs' spot in the upcoming qualifier.

This complete system, from Minor qualifiers to the New Champions Stage, represents several years of fine-tuning and, with 24 teams total, some of the best competition around. This is exemplified in recent years by parity among those teams that become Legends—from Krakow 2017 through Boston 2018, only two teams (Fnatic and SK Gaming ) held onto their Legend status

Given a query and a passage, you must provide a score on an integer scale of 0 to 3 with the following meanings:
0 = represent that the passage has nothing to do with the query, 
1 = represents that the passage seems related to the query but does not answer it, 
2 = represents that the passage has some answer for the query, but the answer may be a bit unclear, or hidden amongst extraneous information and 
3 = represents that the passage is dedicated to the query and contains the exact answer.

Important Instruction: Assign category 1 if the passage is somewhat related to the topic but not completely, category 2 if passage presents something very important related to the entire topic but also has some extra information and category 3 if the passage only and entirely refers to the topic. If none of the above satisfies give it category 0.

Query: You are writing a feature essay for a publication on gaming history and culture. Your task is to analyze the key factors behind the long-term success of Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO).
Passage: Esports Essentials: The Impact of the Counter-Strike Majors

Esports Essentials is a series intended as an introduction to esports for anyone looking to understand the industry.

Counter-Strike has seen almost two decades of competitive play across multiple games. That competition has been headlined by events called Majors—high profile tournaments hosting the world's top teams. These Majors are also a core element to the game's long lifespan, as each year has seen over six figures in prizes across the various Majors.

So, how did Majors come to define top-level Counter-Strike competitions? Here's what you need to know.

What is the History Behind Majors?

There are essentially two eras when it comes to Counter-Strike. The first—better known as the time before the release of the franchise's most recent entry, Global Offensive (CS:GO)—lasted from 2001-2012.

The early years of esports were very different from today; most fans of pro-level play could only hang out in Internet Relay Chat (IRC) channels awaiting results and match replays. Before the rise of livestreaming, watching games live was only really possible in person. Despite all this, the very first Major—the 2001 Cyberathlete Professional League (CPL) Winter Championship—offered $150K in prize money.

CPL established itself with its Winter and Summer Majors, and was soon joined by Korea's World Cyber Games in 2002 and France's Electronic Sports World Cup in 2003. These four tournaments defined Counter-Strike esports through 2007, and contained some of the biggest rivalries between the game's top teams. When CPL folded in 2008, ESL stepped up and added Counter-Strike to its multi-game Intel Extreme Masters (IEM) series. These tournaments continued like clockwork for another four years.

What Changed in 2012?

For one, Global Offensive (CS:GO) was released. This new iteration was finally a strong enough replacement to get players to put down the original version of Counter-Strike, a feat neither of the franchise's previous entries (Condition Zero and Source) could match.

Gaming culture also dramatically shifted in 2012. While streaming gameplay had been possible for a few years (primarily on platforms like Ustream and Justin.tv), the launch of Twitch in 2011 meant big things for gaming. Just three years after it opened its digital doors, Twitch would be in the middle of a bidding war between Amazon and Google, finally selling to the former for $970 million.

The final big change was that Counter-Strike developer Valve got involved in game's esports community. Previously, the game's esports scene was a minor interest to the game's developer—Valve was presumably preoccupied with its other franchises and building out the massive Steam marketplace. But while CS:GO signaled a massive change for the game's player base, it also embodied a massive shift in how the game's developer supported the esports scene.

This shift is seen clearly in the game's 2013 "Arms Deal" update, which added the extremely significant weapon skin system and marketplace. Part of this update, the eSports Weapon Case, hinted at big plans for the game's competitive future:

"A portion of all sales from the eSports Weapon Case will be redirected to fund prize purses at upcoming CS:GO eSport events worldwide."

Several weeks later, the shoe finally dropped. DreamHack announced CS:GO's first Major, a $250K tournament funded in part by those microtransactions. ESL soon rejoined the mix, adding its ESL One Katowice and Cologne stops as Majors as well.

After two successful years, Valve started tapping other organizers to host Majors, starting with Major League Gaming (MLG) in 2016. This change also saw a raise in the prize pool offering to $1 million. Since then, ELEAGUE (2017, 2018), PGL (2017), and FACEIT (2018) have also been asked to host Majors. And, next year, Intel Extreme Masters will host another Major after a seven year break.

It's worth noting that the third-party hosts of Majors shifts every year, based on Valve's discretion. Every year, tournament organizers pitch the developer on who will be hosting one of the two available Majors.

What is the Current Format for a Major?

The most recent format implemented by Valve debuted at ELEAGUE's Boston 2018 Major, and takes part in three stages.

The New Challengers Stage features 16 teams, comprised of the bottom eight teams from the previous Major's New Legends Stage and eight teams from regional qualifiers (known as Minors). Eight teams advance from this stage into the New Legends Stage.

The New Legends Stage features 16 teams, comprised of the top eight teams from the New Challengers Stage and the "Current Legends"—the top eight teams from the previous Major's New Legends Stage. The top eight teams advance once more to the New Champions Stage.

The New Champions Stage features the top eight teams from the New Legends Stage, and is played out in a best-of-three single elimination bracket.
